titleText.es: Supongo que si ella aceptara las realidades irracionales, difícilmente estaría en mis fantasías.
titleText.en: I guess if she accepted irrational realities, she'd hardly be my fantasy.

regions.labelEs: SI HUBIERA ALGUNA MANERA DE QUE PUDIÉRAMOS ESTAR JUNTOS.

applications.explanationEn: Si introduces the wished-for situation, and hubiera presents existence as imagined rather than real.

applications.exampleEs: MANERA DE QUE PUDIÉRAMOS ESTAR JUNTOS
applications.explanationEn: Manera de que introduces the result the imagined way would permit; pudiéramos marks that ability as hypothetical, and estar juntos supplies the possible action and state.

regions.labelEs: TENEMOS TANTA SUERTE DE TENERNOS EL UNO AL OTRO. A TODO ESTO, ¿CÓMO EMPEZÓ?

applications.explanationEn: Tenemos identifies the fortunate people, suerte names the good fortune, and de connects it to tenernos, whose action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Nos is attached to the end of tener, the unchanged -er form, and supplies the people received by the action.
The full four-word expression makes the reciprocal relationship between the two people explicit.
The three words form a transition that reconnects the conversation before the following question.

regions.labelEs: NO, EN SERIO, ¿CÓMO ACABAMOS JUNTOS? ES DIFÍCIL IMAGINARLO SUCEDIENDO.

applications.explanationEn: En and serio form the fixed conversational expression that signals a sincere, non-joking question.
Acabamos names the resulting outcome for “we,” and juntos is the state in which they ended up.
Es difícil supplies the general judgment, while imaginarlo is the unchanged -ar action being judged.
Lo is attached to imaginar, the unchanged -ar form, and supplies the thing imagined.

regions.labelEs: SÍ QUE PONE A PRUEBA LOS LÍMITES DE LA FANTASÍA...

applications.explanationEn: Sí que adds strong confirmation before pone, the verb whose truth is being emphasized.
Pone a prueba supplies the testing expression, and los límites fills its role as the thing being tested.
Eso es is used as a complete reaction recognizing the preceding idea as the answer.

regions.labelEs: DIOS MÍO, ES LA ÚNICA EXPLICACIÓN: SOMOS OBJETOS EN ALGUNA FANTASÍA TRANSITORIA. ¡DESAPARECEREMOS EN CUANTO TERMINE!

applications.explanationEn: Dios mío is the complete emotional exclamation used before the speaker's realization.
The full verb keeps desaparecer and adds the future ending -emos for “we.”
Desapareceremos states the later future result; en cuanto introduces its future trigger, and termine uses the special form for an ending that has not happened yet.
Perder keeps its full dictionary form and adds -é for a future action by “I.”
Perder keeps its full dictionary form and adds -ás for a future action by informal singular “you.”

regions.labelEs: BIEN, NO ME VOY A IR SIN HACER RUIDO. VOY A QUEMAR ESTE PUTO MUNDO.

applications.explanationEn: Voy changes for the speaker, a links to the planned action, and ir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Sin introduces the action that is absent, and hacer remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
Hacer and ruido form the conventional Spanish pairing for making noise.
Voy changes for the speaker, a links to the planned action, and quemar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Quema is the positive informal command addressed to one person, formed from quemar.
Limpiar keeps its full dictionary form and adds -é for a future action by “I.”

excludedUnits.rationale: These two question-mark symbols show the character's silent confusion and are not Spanish lexical words.

cards.questionEn: How can you begin a wish about a situation that is not real now?
cards.answerEn: Use si followed by a special past-looking verb form such as tuviera or hubiera.
cards.noteEn: Si means “if.” For an unreal present wish, the next verb takes a form often ending in -ra: tener becomes tuviera, and haber becomes hubiera. This form is called the imperfect subjunctive; in this use it marks the situation as imagined, not a claim about the past. The wish can stand alone as an exclamation.

example.en: If only I had more time!

cards.answerEn: there were; there existed, in an unreal or wished-for situation
cards.noteEn: Hubiera is a special form of haber used when existence is imagined rather than presented as fact. After si, it often introduces a wish or an unreal condition.

example.en: If only there were a solution!

cards.noteEn: With an imagined or uncertain possibility, alguna can have the natural English sense “any.” It is feminine because it describes a feminine noun, such as idea or manera.

cards.promptEs: una manera de que alguien haga algo
cards.questionEn: How do you describe a way that would let someone do something?
cards.answerEn: Use una manera de que, then name the person and put their action in the special form used for a desired or merely possible result.
cards.noteEn: Manera names the way, and de que introduces the result it would make possible. When that result is wanted, searched for, or hypothetical rather than stated as a fact, Spanish changes the action verb: participan becomes participen, and pueden becomes puedan. This special form is called the subjunctive.

example.es: Buscamos una manera de que todos participen.
example.en: We are looking for a way for everyone to participate.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links manera to the result it would make possible
cards.noteEn: In una manera de que..., de joins “a way” to a clause describing what that way would allow.

example.es: Buscamos una manera de que todos participen.
example.en: We are looking for a way for everyone to participate.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: we could; we might be able to, in an imagined situation
cards.noteEn: Pudiéramos is a special form of poder used for a hypothetical possibility involving “we.” Compare podemos, “we can,” for a possibility presented as real now.

cards.answerEn: to be (in a state or condition)
cards.noteEn: Estar is the unchanged dictionary form used for states, conditions, and locations. After another conjugated verb, estar itself remains unchanged.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is lucky to do or have something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of tener, then suerte de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Tener changes to match the lucky person: tengo suerte, tienes suerte, tenemos suerte. De connects that good fortune to the action. The following action stays in its dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as vivir.

example.en: We are lucky to live here.

cards.answerEn: to; in being, after tener suerte
cards.noteEn: Tener suerte uses de before the action or circumstance that is fortunate.

example.en: I am lucky to live here.

cards.answerEn: to have each other; to have us
cards.noteEn: The action word tener means “to have.” The attached nos normally means “us”; when the same two or more people both do and receive the action, context gives it the reciprocal sense “each other.”

example.en: It is good to have each other nearby.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you make it explicit that two people do something to each other?
cards.answerEn: Use el uno al otro for two masculine people or a mixed pair; change the endings when the people are feminine.
cards.noteEn: The expression literally pairs “the one” with “the other.” Use la una a la otra for two feminine people. It often appears with nos, se, or another small object word when the verb needs one.

example.es: Nos ayudamos el uno al otro.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

cards.answerEn: part of a todo esto: by the way; speaking of that
cards.noteEn: This a belongs to the fixed transition a todo esto rather than marking a destination.

example.en: By the way, what time is it?

cards.questionEn: What does a todo esto do when someone changes or reconnects the topic?
cards.answerEn: It means “by the way,” “speaking of that,” or “after all that.”
cards.noteEn: Speakers use a todo esto to introduce a thought prompted by what came before, often a question that has just occurred to them. Its meaning comes from the whole expression, not by translating its three words separately.

example.es: A todo esto, ¿cuándo empieza la reunión?
example.en: By the way, when does the meeting start?

cards.answerEn: part of a todo esto: by the way; speaking of that
cards.noteEn: Inside this fixed transition, todo does not simply mean “all” on its own.

example.en: By the way, what time is it?

cards.answerEn: part of a todo esto: by the way; speaking of that
cards.noteEn: Inside this fixed transition, esto points back loosely to the topic before introducing a related thought.

example.en: By the way, what time is it?

cards.noteEn: Eh can fill a pause while a speaker thinks or reacts. Its tone and punctuation determine whether it sounds hesitant, surprised, or attention-getting.

example.en: Um... I need to think about it.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.noteEn: This is a present form of recordar. With no before it, no recuerdo means “I don't remember.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en serio (“seriously”)

cards.questionEn: How do you ask whether someone is really serious or whether something is actually true?
cards.answerEn: Use en serio to mean “seriously,” “really,” or “for real.”
cards.noteEn: En serio is a fixed expression. In a question, ¿En serio? often reacts with surprise or disbelief; in a statement, it can contrast sincerity with joking.

example.en: Are you really going to run tomorrow?

cards.answerEn: we ended up; we finished in a resulting state
cards.noteEn: Acabamos can mean “we finish,” but followed directly by a word describing a state, it tells the final condition that resulted.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something ended up in a particular state?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of acabar followed directly by a word that describes the final state.
cards.noteEn: Acabar often means “to finish.” Without de and followed by a state word, it can instead describe the condition that resulted: acabó vacío means it ended up empty. The state word changes for gender and number when it is an adjective: vacía, vacíos, or vacías.
Spanish can begin an impersonal evaluation with es plus a describing word. English normally supplies an impersonal ‘it,’ but Spanish does not add a separate subject word.

example.en: It is strange that it is raining.

cards.questionEn: How do you evaluate an action as easy, difficult, important, or similar?
cards.answerEn: Use es, then the describing word, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Es presents a general judgment, such as es fácil or es difícil. The action being judged stays in its dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir: aprender, salir, imaginar. There is no separate “it” before es in Spanish.

example.en: It is easy to learn with practice.

cards.noteEn: The opposite is fácil, ‘easy.’ Difícil keeps its written accent in the singular.
Imaginar is the unchanged dictionary form “to imagine.” The attached lo means “it” and names what is being imagined.

cards.answerEn: really does; indeed, as part of sí que
cards.noteEn: The accent distinguishes affirmative sí from conditional si, “if.” Before que and a changed verb, sí adds strong confirmation rather than answering a yes-or-no question by itself.

example.en: Ana really does work a lot.

cards.questionEn: How do you strongly confirm that something really is true?
cards.answerEn: Put sí que before the changed verb to mean “really does,” “certainly is,” or “indeed.”
cards.noteEn: The accent on sí matters: sí confirms, while si without an accent means “if.” Que is part of this emphatic pattern and does not need a separate “that” in English. The following verb still changes normally for the person and time.

example.en: Marta really does know how to cook.

cards.answerEn: part of sí que, which strongly confirms what follows
cards.noteEn: In this pattern, que works with sí to add emphasis; it does not introduce an English “that” clause.

cards.answerEn: puts; subjects, as part of poner a prueba
cards.noteEn: Pone is a form of poner. In poner a prueba, the expression means to test someone or something.

example.es: El viaje pone a prueba su paciencia.

cards.promptEs: poner algo o a alguien a prueba
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something tests a person, ability, or limit?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of poner, name what is tested, and add a prueba; the position of the tested item can vary.
cards.noteEn: Poner is literally “to put,” but poner a prueba is the conventional expression “to test” or “to put to the test.” With a person, Spanish normally marks that person with a: poner a Marta a prueba. With a thing, the thing can follow poner directly.

example.es: Este problema pone a prueba nuestra paciencia.

cards.answerEn: part of poner a prueba: to test
cards.noteEn: In the fixed expression poner a prueba, a has no useful separate English translation.

example.es: La pregunta me pone a prueba.

cards.answerEn: test; part of poner a prueba, to test
cards.noteEn: Prueba is “test,” and with poner a it forms the conventional expression poner a prueba.

example.es: La pregunta me pone a prueba.

cards.answerEn: that, in the reaction eso es: that's it
cards.noteEn: Eso normally points to an idea or thing as “that.” In the reaction eso es, it identifies an explanation or answer as the right one.

cards.questionEn: What can you say when you suddenly recognize the right answer or explanation?
cards.answerEn: Say ¡Eso es! to mean “That's it!” or “Exactly!”
cards.noteEn: This short reaction confirms that the idea just mentioned is the answer. It is more idiomatic than translating eso and es separately in this use.

cards.answerEn: is, in the reaction eso es: that's it
cards.noteEn: This form of ser combines with eso in a conventional reaction that recognizes the answer or realization.

Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’
Dios mío can express shock, frustration, or a literal address to God. Mío follows Dios and agrees with its masculine form.

cards.answerEn: we are (an identity or defining description)
cards.noteEn: Somos is the present form of ser used with nosotros or nosotras, “we.” Ser presents an identity, category, or defining description; estamos normally presents a state or location instead.
The ending -emos added to desaparecer marks a future action by “we.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one future action will happen as soon as another one happens?
cards.answerEn: Use a future statement, then en cuanto and a special form of the action that has not happened yet.
cards.noteEn: En cuanto means “as soon as.” When the event after it is still in the future, Spanish uses a special verb form called the subjunctive: llega becomes llegue, and termina becomes termine. The other clause can use the future, as in llamaré, to say what will happen then. For a habitual fact, use the ordinary present instead.

example.en: I will call you as soon as I arrive.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en cuanto, 'as soon as'
no separate English word; completes en cuanto, 'as soon as'
it ends; it finishes, referring to a future event after en cuanto
cards.noteEn: Termine is a special form of terminar used because the ending has not happened yet. Spanish commonly uses this form after en cuanto when looking forward to a future event.

example.en: I will leave as soon as it ends.

cards.noteEn: The ending -é added to perder marks a future action by “I.”
The ending -ás added to perder marks a future action by informal singular “you.”
With a form of ir, me can mark irse, which can mean “to leave” rather than simply “to go.”

example.en: I am going to leave soon.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)

cards.noteEn: Ir normally means “to go.” With a matching small pronoun, as in me voy a ir or nos vamos a ir, it can express leaving.

example.en: We are going to leave early.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does one thing without doing another?
cards.answerEn: Put sin before the second action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. When the same person performs both actions, Spanish uses sin directly before that form; it does not add a word equivalent to English “-ing.”

example.en: She left without closing the door.

cards.noteEn: Hacer can mean creating or producing a physical thing. This is distinct from its very common sense “to do.”

example.en: We are going to make a table.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “to make noise” in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacer followed by ruido.
cards.noteEn: Spanish conventionally pairs hacer, “to make or do,” with ruido, “noise.” Hacer changes for the person and time: hago ruido, hacen ruido, hizo ruido.

example.en: The neighbors make a lot of noise.

cards.noteEn: Before a noun, puto can add strong anger or contempt rather than describing a literal property. It is offensive or very informal, so avoid it in polite settings.

cards.answerEn: burn; an informal command to one person
cards.noteEn: For the affirmative informal command of a regular -ar verb, use the same form as the ordinary él/ella present: quemar becomes quema.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.answerEn: I will clean; I will cleanse
cards.noteEn: The ending -é added to limpiar marks a future action by “I.” In a dramatic context, clean can carry the stronger sense “cleanse.”

example.en: I will clean the kitchen tomorrow.
